text: You already know how to write one Deployment manifest and apply it with kubectl. But the moment that same app needs to run in dev, staging, and production, plain YAML starts to hurt. This lesson is about why Helm exists, and it's the same problem the Terraform course already solved once for infrastructure code — now we're solving it for Kubernetes manifests.

Picture three files: deployment-dev.yaml, deployment-staging.yaml, deployment-prod.yaml, ninety-five percent identical. Every real change — a new image tag, an added environment variable, a bumped resource limit — has to be made correctly, in the right file, three separate times. Miss one, and your environments quietly drift apart with no diff, no history, and no reliable answer to 'what's actually running in prod right now.'

Here's what that looks like on disk: three nearly-identical specs, where the only real differences are a replica count and an image tag, buried in the middle of otherwise-duplicated YAML. A shell script that seds values in before kubectl apply just turns this into an undocumented, fragile templating engine you built yourself, with none of the safety net.

Helm replaces that script with a real templating layer. A chart's templates directory holds manifests written with placeholders like Values dot replicaCount and Values dot image dot tag instead of hardcoded numbers. The template itself never changes between environments — only the values fed into it at install or upgrade time do. One template, many value sets, zero copy-pasted YAML.

That's the core idea: separate the shape of your Deployment from the numbers that customize it per environment, exactly the way Terraform separates a resource block from its variable files. It also means your release history finally has something real to point at — one chart, one set of templates, with every environment's specific numbers tracked as values instead of buried inside duplicated YAML. Next lesson, you'll build a complete chart for a real application — Chart.yaml, values.yaml, a templates folder, and the helper functions that keep your templates from repeating themselves.
